node.label: C. Vann Woodward
node.date_label: Origins of the New South (1951) · Reunion and Reaction (1951) · The Strange Career of Jim Crow (1955) · “The Future of the Past”: presidential address delivered (1969)
node.description: A historian of the American South whose work challenged accounts of an unchanging racial order. Bertram Wyatt-Brown’s substantive memorial presents The Strange Career of Jim Crow as an argument about the historical formation of segregation, while noting later revisions and declining scholarly influence. Woodward’s own presidential address argues that historians should expose anachronisms and mediate between aspirations and historical constraints. The entry keeps that civic role distinct from endorsing a consoling national past or treating a once influential interpretation as settled.
node.representative_figures_and_works: Origins of the New South (1951); Reunion and Reaction (1951; later editions with new prefaces); The Strange Career of Jim Crow (1955; repeatedly revised); “The Future of the Past,” presidential address (delivered 1969).
node.scope_note: New identity is Comer Vann Woodward, not another Woodward dissertation author. Named substantive reader supports the bounded book argument; own address supports civic-method claim. No King quotation, unchecked lecture date, whole-book reading or settled periodization claim. Book revisions and address delivery/publication remain distinct.

proposed_edges.relationship: Historicizes the formation of segregation rather than accepting Jim Crow as an unchanging Southern inheritance.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Named substantive reader Bertram Wyatt-Brown’s discussion of Strange Career; his account is kept separate from a fresh reading of Woodward’s book. Later revisions, competing documentary readings and changing scholarly reception remain explicit.

proposed_edges.relationship: Proposes a civic role for historians in exposing anachronisms and assessing aspirations against historical constraints.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Own address, final paragraphs beginning with the critique of a purposeful or usable past through the concluding defence of historical inquiry, read. This supports a specific account of public responsibility, not a causal claim about a political movement or an endorsement of nostalgia.
